title: £45 a Year for 9,000 Years: Arthur Guinness at St James's Gate
dek: On the last day of 1759 a brewer from Leixlip took a small, disused Dublin brewery in a struggling trade, on a lease of nine thousand years.

story.event: Signing the 9,000-year lease on a disused brewery at St James's Gate, Dublin
story.summary: On 31 December 1759 Arthur Guinness, aged 34, who had run a small brewery in Leixlip with a £100 bequest from his godfather, signed a 9,000-year lease at £45 a year on a small, disused brewery at St James's Gate in Dublin, at a time when the city's brewers were hurt by lower-taxed English beer. He brewed ale first, turned to porter from the 1770s and stopped brewing ale in 1799; the company later bought the land outright.
paragraphs: On 1 December 1759, Arthur Guinness, then 34, signed his name as a new brewer in the minute book of Dublin's corporation of brewers and maltsters. On 31 December he signed a lease on a brewery at St James's Gate in Dublin. The Guinness Archive describes it as small, disused and ill-equipped: four acres with a copper, a kieve, a mill, two malthouses, stabling for twelve horses and a loft for 200 tons of hay. The lease ran for 9,000 years, at a rent of £45 a year.

He came from Leixlip, in County Kildare. His father, Richard, was land steward to Arthur Price, Archbishop of Cashel, and supervised the brewing of beer for the estate's workers, which the archive thinks is probably where his son learnt the craft. The archbishop, Arthur's godfather, left him £100, and with it he ran a small brewery in Leixlip. In 1759 he left that brewery to his younger brother and went to try the capital.

The trade he was entering was in difficulty. English beer was taxed less heavily than Irish, which hurt the city's brewers, and the beer writer Roger Protz counted about thirty other breweries in the St James's Gate area alone. The site had reverted to its owners, the Rainsford family, in 1750 and stood unused. The archive says only that Guinness was not deterred. It gives no reason for the length of the term; Protz read it as confidence in the future.

He began with ale, and within eight years was Master of the brewers' corporation. In the 1770s, as porter from London found favour in Dublin, he started brewing it himself, and in 1799 he stopped brewing ale altogether. The lease's terms mattered later, too. It gave him free access to water, and in 1775, when Dublin Corporation sent the sheriff and a body of men to cut off his supply, he seized a pick-axe from one of them; the archive records that he won his point. The lease no longer applies, because the company later bought the land outright, and the brewery grew to more than fifty acres around the original four.

quote.text: By means of the stock that thou hast, O son, profit can be acquired; what profit accrueth to him who consumeth his stock himself?
quote.locator: Chapter IX, "Concerning Repentance", Sadi's Rebuke from a Camel-Driver
quote.source_title: The Bustān of Sadi, tr. A. Hart Edwards, Project Gutenberg eBook #60471
quote.connection: Saadi meant the hours of a life when he warned that stock consumed earns nothing. Arthur's stock was small and specific: a godfather's £100, a craft learnt on an estate, and a run-down site in a struggling trade. The record shows each of them put to work.

reflection: Arthur Guinness did not pick an easy moment. The tax favoured his rivals, the site was empty and the competition was crowded into the same streets. What he had was a craft, a small sum and a place to work, and he kept using them for forty years before making the change the brewery is now known for.

There may be days when your own field feels too crowded or too hard to start in. This story suggests beginnings can be modest and long. It also shows that the terms agreed at the start, like his water, can matter decades later, which makes them worth reading slowly on a fresh morning.
invitation: Find one agreement your work depends on and read it through once today. Note the single line you would most want to defend if someone came to cut off your supply.

cross_checks.claim: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on the St James's Gate brewery on 31 December 1759 at an annual rent of £45

In 1775 Guinness defended the water rights granted by the 1759 lease against Dublin Corporation

research_notes: Rent: every source checked gives £45 a year for 9,000 years (Guinness Archive fact sheet, Guinness Storehouse, The Irish Times 2004, The Morning Advertiser 2009, Come Here To Me). The £100: the Guinness Archive and Storehouse say Archbishop Price's £100 bequest funded the Leixlip brewery; Come Here To Me (drawing on Lynch and Vaizey, 1960) and Wikipedia (citing Mansfield, 2009) also say the Rainsfords took £100 up front for the St James's Gate lease. The story mentions only the bequest and the £45 rent and does not assert a down payment. Water dispute: the Archive says he 'won his point' and kept a free supply; Wikipedia, citing Bill Yenne (2007), says the matter went to court and in 1785 he agreed to pay £10 a year for water. The story says only that the archive records he won his point in 1775. Disuse: the Archive calls the brewery disused; Come Here To Me says it came back to the Rainsfords in 1750; the story says it reverted in 1750 and stood unused. The 'about thirty other breweries' figure is Roger Protz's and attributed to him, as is the reading of the 9,000-year term as confidence; no Guinness source gives a reason for the term. The 1 December minute-book signature is from the Archive fact sheet, which gives the day without repeating the year; in context it is 1759, before the 31 December lease. Arthur's age of 34 follows the Archive; his exact birth date is uncertain. Funding is marked bootstrapped: the money came from a bequest and his own brewing, with no outside investors recorded. The Guinness Archive fact sheets and FAQ are cited from Internet Archive copies because the live PDFs have moved. The Saadi passage is a spiritual exhortation about using one's life well before the Resurrection; it is applied here by analogy.
